::: {.cite-bar .domain-war-powers}
[In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Pub. L. 79-264]{.cite} [59 Stat. 619]{.cite} [22 U.S.C. 287-287e]{.cite}
:::

Governs U.S. participation in the United Nations: how representatives are appointed, how the United States carries out Security Council decisions, and the terms on which U.S. forces may be made available to the Council.

## Key provisions

- Sec. 5 (22 U.S.C. 287c): the President may implement Security Council measures not involving armed force, such as sanctions, with criminal penalties for violations.
- Sec. 6: agreements to place forces at the Council's disposal under Article 43 of the Charter require congressional approval. No such agreement has ever been concluded.
- Sec. 7 (added 1949): allows detail of up to 1,000 personnel to U.N. activities in noncombatant roles.

## Why it matters

It sits at the center of the question whether a Security Council resolution can substitute for congressional authorization, argued over Korea in 1950 and Libya in 2011. Section 5 is also a sanctions authority that operates next to [IEEPA](ieepa-1977.qmd).

## Current status

In force.
